Pregnancy

Miscarriage pain: symptoms, care and recovery

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy loss can bring physical pain and many emotions, whatever the stage. Some early losses happen before a missed period, and others after a positive test or scan. Pain and bleeding do not by themselves confirm miscarriage: an ongoing pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy or another condition may cause them. This guide mainly concerns early miscarriage; later loss needs a plan with the maternity team.

Start with safety, not a pain score

Get urgent pregnancy-care advice for bleeding, unusual discharge or fluid leakage, or concerning pain if you are pregnant or could be pregnant. Even light bleeding deserves assessment. A clinician may use ultrasound and pregnancy-hormone tests, sometimes repeated, to establish the location and what is happening before recommending miscarriage treatment.

Heavy bleeding that quickly soaks a pad, severe or worsening abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting, marked dizziness, loss of consciousness or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency assessment. Possible ectopic pregnancy can cause internal bleeding without vaginal bleeding or a previous positive test. Do not wait to soak a particular number of pads for two hours, develop every symptom or reach a scheduled appointment; do not drive if faint or seriously unwell.

1. Lower abdominal cramps

During a confirmed miscarriage, the uterus contracts to pass pregnancy tissue and its lining. Cramps may come in waves, ease between episodes or feel like strong period pains in the lower abdomen or pelvis. Intensity varies with the person, stage and management; mild pain does not prove the loss is complete, and severe pain should not be dismissed as expected.

Ask for a pain-relief plan. Paracetamol/acetaminophen may be appropriate; if the pregnancy might still be ongoing, do not self-start ibuprofen or other NSAIDs. After a confirmed loss, a team may recommend ibuprofen if suitable, depending on treatment, health and other medicines. Follow the exact instructions, avoid duplicate ingredients and ask if pain is not controlled. A comfortably warm cloth-wrapped compress may help; avoid burns, overheating or sleeping with heat, and never use comfort measures to delay assessment.

2. Vaginal bleeding and discomfort

Bleeding may be heavier than a usual period and can include clots or tissue, but the amount and duration vary. It is more than an ordinary period following a late cycle; the appearance of tissue cannot reliably establish the diagnosis or exclude ectopic pregnancy. Use pads during the loss so the bleeding can be monitored, and follow the team’s advice about avoiding tampons or menstrual cups.

Change pads regularly and gently clean the outside with water; do not douche or put cleansers or remedies inside the vagina. Foul-smelling discharge, fever, chills or worsening pelvic pain needs urgent assessment now for infection or retained tissue, rather than assuming a yeast infection. Heavy rapid bleeding or feeling faint makes it an immediate emergency. Ask about resuming sex after symptoms have settled and follow your discharge advice.

3. Nausea, diarrhoea or vomiting

Hormonal changes or medicines used to manage a miscarriage can cause nausea, diarrhoea or vomiting. They can also have other causes. Gastrointestinal symptoms do not confirm miscarriage, and bowel discomfort with possible pregnancy can occur with ectopic pregnancy. Persistent symptoms or feeling increasingly ill need assessment.

Take small frequent sips and small meals as tolerated. Plain rice, banana, oats, well-cooked eggs or chicken may suit you, but no particular food is required. If you cannot keep fluids down, urinate much less or become dizzy or weak, seek urgent advice; loss of consciousness, severe pain or marked illness needs emergency care. Ask about prescribed anti-sickness treatment or diarrhoea management rather than taking medicines yourself.

4. Lower back pain

Uterine cramps can be felt in the lower back as well as the abdomen. Pain may range from mild aching to severe discomfort; not every back pain is caused by miscarriage. Tell the team about new, persistent or worsening pain and any urinary symptoms, fever or other changes.

The agreed pain relief and a safely wrapped warm compress may help uncomplicated cramps. Rest when needed and change position gently if comfortable. If pain is severe, increasing or not relieved by the plan, seek prompt assessment; do not assume you must endure it because a loss has been diagnosed. Severe pain with bleeding, faintness or major illness needs immediate emergency care.

5. Shoulder-tip or one-sided pain

Pain at the tip of the shoulder may be a sign of internal bleeding from an ectopic pregnancy, rather than an ordinary part of miscarriage. New shoulder-tip pain or one-sided pelvic pain with possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment now, even without visible bleeding or a positive test. Rectal pressure, painful bowel movements or pelvic discomfort may also occur and should be reported.

Sudden or severe abdominal/pelvic pain, shoulder pain with bleeding or faintness, marked dizziness, loss of consciousness or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for a home test or try to settle these symptoms with pain medicine, heat or water. A previously suspected miscarriage does not safely explain every new pain.

6. Weakness, tiredness or headache

Physical strain, disrupted sleep and emotional distress can leave you tired, but weakness may also reflect blood loss, anaemia, dehydration or infection. A headache or fatigue is not automatically harmless after a loss. Tell a clinician if symptoms are new, persistent or worsening.

Rest, fluids and nourishing food can support recovery after appropriate assessment, but they do not treat dangerous bleeding or infection. Marked dizziness, fainting, breathlessness, racing heartbeat with illness or inability to stand safely needs urgent assessment; loss of consciousness, severe breathlessness or faintness with heavy bleeding is an immediate emergency. Ask whether examination or blood tests are needed.

7. Grief and emotional pain

You may feel sadness, shock, anger, guilt, relief, numbness or fear about another pregnancy, sometimes together or at unexpected times. There is no required emotional response, and how far along the pregnancy was does not determine whether support is deserved. Partners and other close people can be affected too.

Talking with trusted people, a counsellor, a pregnancy-loss support group or a mental-health professional may help. Grief and depression are not identical, but depression, anxiety or trauma symptoms can follow a loss and are treatable. Estimates from research groups cannot predict your personal risk. Seek care for persistent hopelessness, loss of interest or impaired daily life, and urgent help for self-harm or suicidal thoughts. Immediate danger or inability to stay safe needs local emergency services or an emergency department now.

Choosing management after a confirmed loss

If no tissue remains and you are well, further treatment may not be needed. Otherwise, options for early miscarriage include expectant management (waiting with a clinical plan) medicines to help tissue pass, or a procedure, often suction aspiration. Surgical management is sometimes called evacuation or D&C; discuss the actual technique and anaesthesia rather than assuming every procedure is the same.

Choice depends on symptoms, gestation, scan findings, health, preferences and available services. Heavy bleeding or infection can make urgent hospital treatment necessary. Ask about expected pain and bleeding, side effects, emergency contact arrangements and what happens if the first option is unsuccessful. Waiting is not simply ignoring symptoms, and there is no single pain level or timetable that fits everyone.

Bleeding, follow-up and the next period

After an early loss, bleeding often gradually lessens over one to two weeks; it can last longer with some management approaches. Do not automatically regard spotting until the next period as normal. Contact the team for persistent, increasing or prolonged bleeding or pain, fever, foul discharge or ongoing pregnancy symptoms; seek emergency care for the warning signs above.

Follow the test and review plan: NICE advises a home pregnancy test around three weeks after expectant or medical management, with review if positive. A negative result does not dismiss persistent bleeding, pelvic pain or fever. Repeat ultrasound or other tests may be needed, rather than a scan being mandatory for everyone. Periods often return in four to eight weeks, but timing varies; ask when to contact the team if yours does not return. Ovulation can occur first, so discuss contraception if pregnancy is not wanted.

Recovery is individual

Some feel physically better in days, while others need weeks or longer depending on the loss, treatment and complications. There is no universal two- or three-week deadline for recovery or a requirement to return to work before you feel ready. Ask for practical help, time off or a review if recovery is not progressing.

Emotional recovery may take longer than physical recovery, and support can be requested at any stage. Agree when to seek follow-up and which medicines or activities are suitable. Bring notes if helpful, but symptoms and safety take priority over tracking. You deserve care for both the physical and emotional effects, without needing to prove that the pregnancy was far enough along to matter.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

March 2026 NHS advice supports urgent assessment of pregnancy bleeding and immediate emergency care for severe pain, shoulder pain, faintness or heavy bleeding.

NICE NG126, updated June 2026, supports individualized expectant, medical or surgical management and follow-up testing, with reassessment for ongoing symptoms.

Current UCLH information distinguishes pain relief in an uncertain ongoing pregnancy from care after a confirmed loss and highlights infection, bleeding and emotional support.

The older available RCOG and NHS ectopic leaflets are used with their dates acknowledged and corroborated by current clinical advice; grief is not a fixed personal depression-risk percentage.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record symptoms, bleeding changes, medicines, tests and questions for the care team. A record cannot confirm miscarriage, exclude ectopic pregnancy or infection, or decide whether it is safe to wait. Do not delay urgent help to complete it.

When to seek help

Possible pregnancy with new pain, bleeding or shoulder-tip symptoms needs prompt assessment. Heavy rapid bleeding, severe pain, shoulder pain with bleeding or faintness, loss of consciousness or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency care, even without visible bleeding in possible ectopic pregnancy. Fever, foul discharge or worsening pain needs urgent assessment now. Do not rely on a pad threshold, heat, fluids or a negative home test to delay care. Suicidal thoughts need urgent professional help; immediate danger or inability to stay safe requires emergency services now.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pain or bleeding alone cannot diagnose miscarriage or exclude an ectopic pregnancy.
  • Heavy rapid bleeding, severe pain, shoulder pain with bleeding or faintness, or loss of consciousness needs immediate emergency care; do not wait for a pad-count threshold.
  • Pain relief depends on whether the loss is confirmed, the treatment and your health; heat or hydration must not delay assessment.
  • Fever, foul discharge, increasing pain or persistent bleeding needs review, even after a negative pregnancy test.
  • Recovery and grief vary; support is available for both physical symptoms and emotional distress.

Frequently asked questions

What do miscarriage cramps feel like?

They may feel like strong period cramps or waves of pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis. Severity varies. Seek advice for pain in possible pregnancy; severe, one-sided or worsening pain or faintness requires urgent or immediate emergency assessment.

Are nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting normal?

They can occur with hormonal changes or miscarriage medicines, but are not always harmless or caused by a loss. Inability to keep fluids down, reduced urine or worsening illness needs urgent advice; severe pain or loss of consciousness needs emergency care.

Is shoulder pain a miscarriage symptom?

Shoulder-tip pain can warn of internal bleeding from ectopic pregnancy. Get urgent assessment now with possible pregnancy, even without bleeding or a positive test. Shoulder pain with bleeding, severe pain or faintness needs immediate emergency care.

Is weakness or tiredness expected?

Tiredness can occur, but weakness may reflect blood loss, dehydration, anaemia or infection. Report persistent or worsening symptoms. Fainting, severe breathlessness, loss of consciousness or heavy bleeding with marked dizziness needs immediate emergency care.

How much bleeding means I should get help?

Heavy bleeding that quickly soaks a pad, especially with severe pain, dizziness or faintness, needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for two pads an hour for two hours. Even light bleeding during pregnancy warrants urgent pregnancy-care advice.

Can I take ibuprofen for the pain?

If pregnancy could still be ongoing, do not self-start it. After a confirmed miscarriage, a team may recommend it if suitable for your treatment and health. Follow your personal plan and avoid duplicate ingredients; uncontrolled pain needs reassessment.

What follow-up is needed?

Follow the team’s plan for testing and review. A pregnancy test around three weeks after expectant or medical management is commonly advised; a positive result needs review, and negative tests do not dismiss persistent bleeding, pain or fever.

When should I seek emotional support?

Whenever you want it, including sadness, mixed feelings, anxiety or fear about another pregnancy. Persistent hopelessness or difficulty functioning deserves professional care. Suicidal thoughts need urgent help; immediate danger or inability to stay safe needs emergency services or an emergency department now.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
